theme: Hezekiah’s faithfulness; the Assyrian threat; deliverance
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 18:1-20:21. After the fall of Samaria, Judah stands alone against Assyria. Read Hezekiah’s story as a test of what faith does when the empire is at the gate, and notice the sad ending in chapter 20.
settingTheScene: Hezekiah became king of Judah around 715 BC, a few years after Samaria fell. He is one of the best kings in Judah’s history. He removed the high places, destroyed the bronze serpent Moses had made, and trusted the LORD. Assyria, the empire that had swallowed the north, now turned on Judah. This unit follows that crisis from the viewpoint of the king and of the prophet Isaiah, who spoke to him throughout.
observation: “He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that there was none like him among all the kings of Judah after him” (18:5).
“He broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for until those days the people of Israel had made offerings to it” (18:4).
“In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them” (18:13).
The Rabshakeh asks, “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” (18:19).
“Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, The LORD will surely deliver us” (18:30).
Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD and prays (19:14-19).
“For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David” (19:34).
Hezekiah shows the Babylonian envoys all his treasures, and Isaiah says, “Days are coming when all that is in your house… shall be carried to Babylon” (20:12-18).
interpretation:
Hezekiah’s reforms show what real faith looks like in leadership. He did not merely keep the temple clean. He destroyed the bronze serpent, a God-given object that had turned into an idol. Even good things from the past become dangerous when people worship them. The writer says there was none like him in his trust in the LORD.

Then the crisis comes. Sennacherib captures the fortified cities and Hezekiah, at first, tries to buy him off with silver stripped from the temple. It fails. The Assyrian spokesman then delivers a speech designed to break the people’s confidence. He asks the central question: “On what do you rest this trust of yours?” He argues that Egypt is a broken reed, that Hezekiah’s reforms have offended God, and that no god of any nation has ever stopped Assyria. He speaks Hebrew loudly so that the people on the wall will hear. This is psychological warfare.

Hezekiah’s response is the model. He tears his clothes, goes to the temple, and sends to Isaiah. When a threatening letter arrives, he does something striking: he spreads it out before the LORD. He brings the threat into God’s presence and prays that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that the LORD alone is God. God answers through Isaiah and strikes down the Assyrian army in the night.

Chapter 20 turns to Hezekiah’s illness and recovery, and then to a quiet failure. When envoys from Babylon come, he shows them everything, perhaps proud of his wealth, perhaps hoping for an alliance. Isaiah tells him the day will come when it is all carried off to Babylon. Hezekiah responds with a short-sighted relief that there will be peace in his days. The great king who trusted God in the crisis is weaker in prosperity. Faith has to be kept through easy times as well.
connection: Jesus said, “Whoever believes in me will not be put to shame” (Romans 10:11 quotes Isaiah). Hezekiah’s prayer, spreading a trouble before the LORD, anticipates Philippians 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:7. Paul calls on us to “take every thought captive” (2 Corinthians 10:5) against arguments raised against the knowledge of God. The bronze serpent lifted by Moses became a picture of Christ lifted up (John 3:14), but it was not to be worshiped in itself.
application:
Ask whether anything good from your past, a ministry, habit, or tradition, has become something you rely on more than God.

Take a worry or a threatening message and spread it out before the LORD in prayer.

Watch for pride in good times. Ask God for humility when things are going well.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what voices ask you to rest on something else, and say you rest on him.
Spread your fears before him, as Hezekiah spread the letter.
Thank him for the deliverance he has given.
